title: Linear Algebra for Data Science
path: MATH 2ND YEAR/MATH 2303/LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE.md
body:
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) solved systems that have an answer. MATH 2303 handles the
situation data actually produces, where the system has no answer at all.

The reason is a counting mismatch. A dataset has more rows than parameters, so fitting a line
to a thousand points means a thousand equations in two unknowns, and those equations disagree
because the measurements carry noise. There is no line through all thousand points, and the
question changes from solving to approximating: which line comes closest.

Every technique in the course answers that. [[Projection]] replaces solving,
[[Least Squares]] replaces $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, the [[Singular Value Decomposition|SVD]]
replaces [[Diagonalization]], and approximation replaces equality. The course runs algorithms
on real datasets ahead of theory, with two hours a week of [[NumPy]] in the laboratory block.

This is the keystone of the degree's mathematics. It is the only place
[[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]], the SVD and norms as loss functions appear, and the
chain from [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] through the [[Spectral Theorem]] and the SVD to
PCA is the route from the MATH block into [[MACHINE LEARNING]].

One sentence organises everything: when the system has no solution, project.

## Topics

### Projection, and why it is the answer

An [[Inner Product]] keeps the three rules of the [[Dot Product]] and discards the specific
formula, which carries length, angle and orthogonality across to matrices and to functions
where no picture exists.

[[Projection]] drops a vector onto a subspace and splits it into two pieces:

```
b = (3, 4)                      the target
W = the x-axis                  the subspace of reachable points

projection: (3, 0)              the closest reachable point
residual:   (0, 4)              what is left over

the residual is perpendicular to W, and that is what makes (3,0) closest
```

Any other point on the axis is further away, because moving along the axis adds to a leg of a
right triangle whose other leg is fixed at 4. That argument generalises: the closest point of a
subspace is the projection, and the residual is orthogonal to the whole subspace.

For an orthonormal basis the projection is a sum of dot products,
$\text{proj}_W\mathbf{v} = \sum_i (\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i)\mathbf{u}_i$, and for a general
basis it is $P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$. A projection matrix is exactly one that is idempotent,
satisfying $P^2 = P$ because projecting twice changes nothing, and symmetric. Its eigenvalues
are 0 and 1, its rank equals its trace, and $I - P$ projects onto the orthogonal complement.

### Orthonormal bases

[[Orthonormal Basis]] explains what orthogonality is worth paying for. In a general basis,
finding coordinates means solving a system, at $O(n^3)$. In an orthonormal basis each
coordinate is one dot product, and the coefficients can be truncated meaningfully, because
each one carries an independent piece of the vector. A skewed basis has no such property, so
dropping a coefficient there can change the others' meaning.

An orthogonal matrix satisfies $Q^{-1} = Q^T$, preserves lengths and angles, and has
determinant $\pm 1$, making it a rotation or a reflection. [[Gram-Schmidt]] manufactures an
orthonormal basis from any basis by subtracting off projections onto what has already been
built, and bookkeeping that process produces the QR decomposition.

### Norms, and where loss functions come from

[[Vector Norm]] measures size, and different norms measure it differently:

```
v = (3, 4)

L₁ = |3| + |4|        = 7        sum of absolute values
L₂ = √(3² + 4²)       = 5        ordinary distance
L∞ = max(|3|, |4|)    = 4        largest component
```

$L_2$ is the only norm arising from an inner product, which is why it alone has a projection
formula, a closed-form solution and a smooth gradient, and it is why nearly every derivation in
this course is a squared-error derivation.

As a loss, squared $L_2$ is mean squared error and squares the outliers so they dominate the
fit, while $L_1$ is mean absolute error, is robust to outliers, and has no closed form. As a
penalty on the weights of a model, $L_2$ shrinks every coefficient smoothly and $L_1$ drives
some of them to exactly zero, which is why lasso selects features and ridge does not. For
matrices, $\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\sum_k \sigma_k^2}$ and
$\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1$.

### Symmetric matrices

The [[Spectral Theorem]] states that a matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable exactly when it
is symmetric, giving $A = QDQ^T$ with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. Ordinary
[[Diagonalization]] can fail, and this cannot.

That matters because the matrices data produces are symmetric by construction. A covariance
matrix is symmetric because the covariance of $x$ with $y$ equals the covariance of $y$ with
$x$. So are Gram matrices, adjacency matrices of undirected graphs, and Hessians. The
decomposition writes $A = \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T$, a weighted sum of
rank-one projections, so a symmetric matrix is a set of directions each with a scaling factor.

Any $A^TA$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite, since
$\mathbf{x}^TA^TA\mathbf{x} = \|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 \geq 0$, so its eigenvalues are non-negative
and their square roots are the singular values of $A$.

[[Quadratic Form]] covers $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ and reads definiteness off the eigenvalue
signs: all positive gives a minimum, all negative gives a maximum, and mixed signs give a
saddle. Applied to the Hessian that is the multivariable second-derivative test, and it is the
version that survives past two variables where the determinant test in
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] stops.

### The singular value decomposition

The [[Singular Value Decomposition]] writes any matrix as $A = U\Sigma V^T$, with $U$ and $V$
orthogonal and $\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0$ on the diagonal of $\Sigma$. Square
or rectangular, singular or full rank, invertible or not: every matrix has one, which is what
the spectral theorem alone could not deliver.

It is the spectral theorem applied once on each side, with $V$ holding the eigenvectors of
$A^TA$, $U$ holding those of $AA^T$, and $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$. The defining equation
is the eigenvector equation with the input and output directions allowed to differ:

$$
A\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i
$$

which is what lets it apply to a non-square matrix, where input and output live in different
spaces. Geometrically every linear map is a rotation, a stretch and a second rotation, and the
image of the unit sphere is an ellipsoid whose semi-axes are the singular values.

The expansion $A = \sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{v}_i^T$ runs to the rank $r$, and
it hands over orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces. Numerical rank is the
count of singular values above a tolerance, which is a usable definition where exact rank is
not, and the condition number $\sigma_1/\sigma_r$ says how much a small input error is
amplified, which the [[Determinant]] cannot detect.

[[Low-Rank Approximation]] truncates that sum after $k$ terms. Eckart-Young-Mirsky proves the
truncated $A_k$ is the best possible rank-$k$ approximation in both the Frobenius and spectral
norms, with error $\|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}$, the first discarded singular value. That is
an unusually strong statement: no other rank-$k$ matrix does better by either measure, and the
error is known before the approximation is computed. It compresses real data because
correlated columns produce near-dependence, which produces rapidly decaying singular values.

### Principal component analysis

[[Principal Component Analysis]] applies all of the above to one task, reducing the number of
features while keeping as much information as possible.

```
1. centre the data          subtract the mean of each column
2. form the covariance      C = Xᶜᵀ Xᶜ / (n-1),  symmetric by construction
3. eigen-decompose C        directions of greatest variance, with their variances
4. keep the top k           the k directions holding the most variance
5. project onto them        each sample becomes k numbers, down from p
```

Centring is required for step 2 to mean anything, since an uncentred matrix measures distance
from the origin, and covariance measures spread around the mean. In practice the SVD of the centred matrix replaces forming
the covariance explicitly, because squaring the matrix squares the condition number.

The data matrix $X$ is $n \times p$ with samples in rows, which is the one place this vault
departs from treating vectors as columns, so the components are the right singular vectors.
Principal components are uncorrelated by construction, being orthogonal eigenvectors of a
covariance matrix, and maximising retained variance and minimising reconstruction error are
the same optimisation viewed from either end.

Three limits come with it. PCA is sensitive to scale, so a feature measured in millimetres
dominates one measured in metres unless the data is standardised first. It is linear, so it
cannot follow a curved manifold. It is unsupervised, so it never sees the labels, and a
high-variance direction can be irrelevant to what is being predicted.

### Least squares

[[Least Squares]] is the projection argument applied to fitting. The reachable set of
$A\mathbf{x}$ is the column space of $A$, the observed $\mathbf{b}$ lies outside it, and the
closest reachable point is the projection, so the residual is orthogonal to every column:

$$
A^T(\mathbf{b} - A\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = \mathbf{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}
$$

Those are the normal equations, and normal here means perpendicular. No calculus appears
anywhere in the derivation.

Fitting $y = a + bx$ to the points $(1,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,2)$:

```
x̄ = 2,  ȳ = 1.667
b = Σ(x-x̄)(y-ȳ) / Σ(x-x̄)²  =  1.0 / 2.0  =  0.5
a = ȳ - b·x̄                  =  1.667 - 1.0  =  0.667

fitted:     1.167,  1.667,  2.167
residuals: -0.167,  0.333, -0.167     which sum to zero
```

No line passes through all three points, and this one minimises the sum of the squared
residuals. A regression model has to be linear in its coefficients alone, so columns holding
$x^2$ or $\log x$ fit curves through the same machinery. Forming $A^TA$ numerically squares the
condition number, so QR is used in practice, and the SVD when the matrix is rank deficient.

[[Pseudoinverse]] generalises the whole picture. The Moore-Penrose inverse
$A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T$ inverts the non-zero singular values and leaves the zeros in place. It
exists for every matrix and returns the exact solution when there is one, the least squares
fit when there are too many equations, and the minimum-norm solution when there are too few.

### Transforms and images

The [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] converts a data vector into a frequency signature and
appears here as a change of basis. [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) owns the
transform and the [[Fast Fourier Transform]], and this course borrows both.

[[Wavelet Transform]] uses a localised basis, so a coefficient records how much of a frequency
is present and where it occurs, which is what a Fourier coefficient cannot say. That
localisation is what multi-resolution analysis is built on and why modern image compression
uses it.

[[Image Processing]] treats an image as a [[Matrix]] of intensities. Filtering is convolution,
which is a [[Dot Product]] of a small kernel with each patch of the image, and a Sobel kernel
is a discrete derivative, so edge detection is differentiation. Compression is a truncated SVD
with visible results, where dropping the smallest singular values blurs detail before it
destroys structure.

### The laboratory

[[NumPy]] supplies `svd`, `eigh`, `qr`, `lstsq`, `pinv` and `norm`. The laboratory teaches two
habits the theory leaves out: solve a system directly and leave `inv` alone, because it is
slower and less accurate, and vectorise every loop over array elements, because the
same arithmetic runs orders of magnitude faster inside the library.

## Related courses

- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) is the prerequisite for every note here.
  [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] and [[Diagonalization]] feed the [[Spectral Theorem]],
  [[Dot Product]] and [[Basis]] feed [[Projection]] and [[Orthonormal Basis]],
  [[Matrix Inverse]] raises the question about non-square matrices that [[Pseudoinverse]]
  answers, and [[Kernel and Range]] supplies the rank that [[Low-Rank Approximation]] reduces.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) derives [[Least Squares]] a second way as [[Linear Regression]],
  minimising the sum of squared residuals to reach the same equations, where $r^2$ is
  Pythagoras on the resulting right triangle. The covariance matrix PCA decomposes is built
  from [[Variance]] and [[Correlation]], and Pearson's $r$ is the cosine of the angle between
  two centred data vectors.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) reaches the same second-derivative test from the
  [[Multivariable Calculus]] and [[Gradient]] side that [[Quadratic Form]] definiteness gives
  here.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) has [[Orthogonal Functions]], of which
  [[Orthonormal Basis]] here is the finite-dimensional case, and a coordinate is a
  [[Fourier Coefficients|Fourier coefficient]] with the integral replaced by a sum. Its
  [[Convolution Theorem]] is why the filtering in [[Image Processing]] can run in the
  frequency domain.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] use
  [[Principal Component Analysis]] for dimensionality reduction, [[Vector Norm]] for
  [[Loss Function|loss functions]], and [[Gradient Descent]] to minimise one over a surface
  whose local shape is a [[Quadratic Form]]. [[Image Processing]] is the classical half of
  [[Computer Vision]] and the hand-designed ancestor of the [[CNN]].
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) adds structure to a [[Vector Space]] by axioms the way this
  course adds an [[Inner Product]] to one.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] analyses [[Gaussian Elimination]], QR and the SVD, all
  $O(n^3)$ on square inputs, and [[NumPy]]'s vectorisation speedup is the clearest example in
  the vault of constant factors mattering alongside [[Time Complexity]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]] (COMP 1631) is the Python course, and an `ndarray` is
  an [[Array]] carrying a shape.
